steps.say: Bladder pressure is measured against belly pressure during filling. Vesical pressure is recorded from a bladder catheter. Abdominal pressure is taken from a rectal balloon. Detrusor pressure is calculated by subtracting belly from bladder. Artefacts from coughing or straining are removed by the subtraction. True detrusor rises are revealed underneath.
steps.tx: **Detrusor pressure** (bladder muscle pressure), **Pdet** (calculated bladder pressure), is derived during **filling cystometry** (bladder filling test) by subtracting intra-abdominal pressure, **Pabd** (belly pressure via rectal balloon), from total intravesical pressure, **Pves** (whole bladder pressure). Zero both lines to atmosphere and cough check the subtraction, because rectal contractions mimic detrusor overactivity.

steps.say: Compliance is defined as bladder stretchiness over filling. Volume change is divided by pressure change. Delta V over Delta Pdet is calculated for every fill. Values below twelve to twenty are flagged as dangerously low. Stiff low capacity bladders are feared to threaten the kidneys. Compliance is tracked on every fill from start to end.
steps.tx: **Bladder compliance** (stretch per pressure) equals change in volume over change in detrusor pressure, **Delta-V** (volume rise) divided by **Delta-Pdet** (pressure rise), with values below **12 to 20 mL/cmH2O** (twelve to twenty millilitres per centimetre of water) marking dangerously stiff low compliance. Suspect poor compliance with small capacity and rising filling pressures. Protect the upper tracts before pressures climb, because kidneys fail silently.

steps.say: Leak point pressure is staged to predict kidney damage. Detrusor leak point pressure is measured without any catheter strain. Values above forty cm of water are flagged for upper tract harm. Hydronephrosis with secondary renal damage is expected beyond it. Pressures are lowered before damage is established. Clean drainage is maintained to keep DLPP safe.
steps.tx: **Detrusor leak point pressure** (leak pressure), **DLPP** (damage warning pressure), above **40 cmH2O** (forty centimetres of water) in neurogenic bladders predicts **upper tract damage** (kidney harm) with hydronephrosis and secondary renal failure. Keep storage pressures below this line with drainage and therapy. Recheck DLPP after every intervention, because pressures decide prognosis.

steps.say: Strokes above the pons are noted to change bladder control mildly. Suprapontine lesions are followed by detrusor overactivity. The sphincter is still relaxed in a coordinated way. Normal voiding synergy is maintained throughout. Parkinson disease is grouped with stroke lesions here. Urgency with frequency is managed by bladder training.
steps.tx: **Suprapontine lesion** (brain injury above the pons) from stroke or Parkinson disease produces **detrusor overactivity** (uninhibited bladder contractions) with coordinated sphincter relaxation and preserved voiding synergy. Manage urgency and frequency with bladder training and timed voiding. Image the brain when overactivity starts late in life, because new lesions explain new symptoms.

steps.say: Cord injury above the sacrum is staged as outlet war in urodynamics. Suprasacral lesions above T6 are complicated by dyssynergia. Involuntary detrusor contraction is opposed by sphincter closure. Pressures spike against a closed outlet dangerously. Kidneys with continence are both damaged together. Pressures with retention are managed by expert teams.
steps.tx: **Detrusor-sphincter dyssynergia** (bladder versus outlet war), **DSD** (uncoordinated voiding), follows **suprasacral cord injury** (spinal damage above the sacrum), classically cervical or thoracic trauma above **T6** (sixth thoracic level), where detrusor contraction meets sphincter closure and pressures spike. Drain reliably and lower outlet resistance promptly, because sustained high pressures destroy kidneys.

steps.say: High cord lesions are feared to hide a vascular trap. Autonomic dysreflexia is triggered by bladder overdistension. Lesions at or above T6 are charged with this risk lifelong. Paroxysmal hypertension is announced by pounding headache. Bradycardia with sweating above the lesion is documented in the attack. The bladder is drained at once with the patient sat up.
steps.tx: **Autonomic dysreflexia** (cord injury vascular storm) strikes **T6 cord lesion** (spinal damage at or above sixth thoracic) patients when bladder overdistension triggers **paroxysmal hypertension** (sudden severe high pressure) with pounding headache, bradycardia, and diaphoresis above the lesion. Sit the patient up, drain the bladder at once, and remove the trigger. Treat as an emergency, because strokes and fits follow unchecked surges.

vis.alt: Distended bladder triggering autonomic dysreflexia in high cord injury.
vis.caption: Overdistension trigger: drain at once with the patient sat up. Credit: StewardMD.

steps.say: Low lesions are staged to silence the bladder pump. Sacral and infrasacral damage is caused by conus or cauda injury. Pelvic plexus surgery is grouped the same way. The detrusor is left acontractile and never contracted. Compliance stays low with dribbling incontinence. Voluntary sphincter control is recorded as lost alongside.
steps.tx: **Acontractile detrusor** (silent bladder pump) follows sacral and infrasacral lesions of **conus medullaris** (cord tip) or **cauda equina** (horse tail roots), or pelvic plexus surgery, with low compliance and no voluntary sphincter control. Expect retention with overflow dribbling rather than urgency. Manage with scheduled catheterization, because the pump never recovers.

steps.say: Retention with incomplete emptying is managed by scheduled drainage. Clean intermittent catheterization is taught for self care at home. Lapides is credited with introducing the technique decades ago. The bladder is emptied four to six times daily. Sterile technique is not required for clean passes. Kidneys with continence are protected together.
steps.tx: **Clean intermittent catheterization** (timed self catheter passes), **CIC** (Lapides technique) introduced by **Lapides** (catheter pioneer), is the gold standard for incomplete emptying and neuropathic retention. Empty four to six times daily before the bladder overdistends. Teach technique with measured volumes, because residual checks prove adequacy.

vis.alt: Straight catheter used for clean intermittent catheterization.
vis.caption: CIC by Lapides: empty four to six times daily. Credit: StewardMD.
